items.title: Schuren mag! 7x inzichten over democratie en burgerschap
items.raw_text: Een literaire avond in je bibliotheek over een onderwerp dat gevoelig ligt. Een school die een collectie afwijst vanwege levensovertuigingen. Of een gesprek tussen mensen die lijnrecht tegenover elkaar staan… Als bibliotheek ben je er voor iedereen. Maar kun je er eigenlijk wel voor iedereen zijn? En hoe ga je om met meningen die botsen met elkaar, of misschien zelfs met die van jou? Op 24 september gingen zo’n 350 bibliotheekprofessionals hierover met elkaar in gesprek tijdens het Kennisfestival Democratie & Burgerschap , georganiseerd door SPN . items.title: AI-vermeldingen, CAPTCHA en meer: praktische tips voor privacy en informatiebeveiliging
items.raw_text: Privacy en informatiebeveiliging blijven actuele onderwerpen voor bibliotheken. Sinds 2 augustus is het bijvoorbeeld verplicht om transparant te zijn over gebruik van AI. items.title: Maak kennis met Constance: de kracht achter de onderwijscollecties
items.raw_text: Tussen de boekenkasten in het collectiegebouw van Rijnbrink werkt Constance Melissen. Als collectiebeheerder Onderwijs zorgt zij ervoor dat scholen boeken krijgen die aansluiten bij hun lessen én de leefwereld van kinderen en jongeren. Zo draagt ze bij aan leesplezier bij de jeugd. In dit artikel maak je kennis met Constance en het werk dat zij doet. Wie regelmatig op een basisschool komt, herkent het meteen: de themahoek. Vaak vol met boeken in een bepaald thema. Soms door de leerkracht aangevuld met accessoires. Een thema is bijvoorbeeld kerst, of vervoer. Maar ook duurzaamheid of sprookjes. Bij Rijnbrink noemen we dit onderwijscollecties. De boeken zijn verzameld rondom een thema. Ze sluiten aan bij de leefwereld van kinderen en passen bij het niveau van verschillende leeftijdsgroepen in het basisonderwijs en de kinderopvang. Zo ontdekken kinderen nieuwe onderwerpen en lezen ze boeken die aansluiten bij hun interesses en ontwikkeling. Ook helpt het de leraren bij het geven van hun lessen. items.title: Frisse financiële start in 2027? 5x tips voor jouw jaarafsluiting

items.title: Op weg naar slimmer en duurzamer transport
items.raw_text: We merken het allemaal aan de pomp: de prijs van brandstof is hoog. Maandelijks betaalt Rijnbrink nu €3.000 meer aan brandstof dan een jaar geleden. Het is daarom noodzakelijk om efficiënt en duurzaam te rijden. Misschien merk je dat als bibliotheek of school, omdat we materialen op een andere tijd bezorgen dan je gewend bent. items.title: Prinsjesdag 2026: 5 thema’s uitgelicht voor bibliotheken
items.raw_text: Prinsjesdag 2026 zit erop. De nieuw gepresenteerde plannen laten zien dat het kabinet vertrouwen heeft in de toekomst van bibliotheken. Er komt meer zekerheid voor leesbevordering, bibliotheken krijgen een belangrijke maatschappelijke rol en er is geld voor verdere ontwikkeling. Tegelijkertijd zijn er ook uitdagingen. Gaby Erckens, onze teamleider Financiën en Control, dook in de plannen en zette de belangrijkste 5 thema’s op een rij. 1. Structureel geld voor leesbevordering Goed nieuws is dat de programma’s BoekStart en de Bibliotheek op school vanaf 2027 structurele financiering krijgen. Dat betekent dat je als bibliotheek of school niet langer afhankelijk bent van tijdelijke subsidies. Voor 2027 is hiervoor €38 miljoen beschikbaar. Vanaf 2028 groeit dit naar €50 miljoen per jaar. Bibliotheken en scholen kunnen dus langdurige plannen maken en blijven investeren in leesplezier, taalontwikkeling en onderwijs. 2. items.title: Lezen dichter bij studenten: de kracht van samenwerken

items.title: Vacature directeur / bestuurder

items.title: Nederlanders denken dat ze phishing herkennen, maar AI maakt oplichting steeds echter en juist dát is een groot veiligheidsrisico
items.raw_text: Uit het jaarlijkse nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, mede mogelijk gemaakt door het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, blijkt dat Nederlanders wél weten wat veilig online gedrag is, maar gemiddeld slechts een derde van de veilige handelingen consequent toepassen. Den Haag – Nederlanders weten goed hoe ze zich online moeten beschermen, maar vertrouwen opvallend vaak op hun eigen vermogen om gevaar te herkennen. Zodra er meer van hen gevraagd wordt dan kijken, neemt de motivatie om zich veilig te gedragen af. Zo kunnen criminelen met een gestolen wachtwoord niet zomaar een account overnemen. En maar drie op de tien gaan altijd zelf naar de officiële website in plaats van op een link te klikken. Dat blijkt uit het nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, dat vandaag verschijnt bij de start van de Europese cybersecuritymaand. Wie denkt zelf phishing te herkennen, slaat in veel gevallen de stappen over die je écht beschermen. items.title: Van regisserende naar ontwerpende overheid

Op 24 juni vond in Amare voor de vijfde keer de CIO-dag plaats. items.title: OTC Whitepaper Soevereiniteit
items.raw_text: Digitale soevereiniteit betekent niet dat organisaties alle digitale diensten zelf moeten bezitten of beheren. Het betekent dat zij aantoonbare grip hebben op kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden: inzicht in de keten, bewuste risicoacceptatie, uitvoerbare alternatieven, onafhankelijke controle en transparante communicatie over keuzes en restrisico’s. In het whitepaper over digitale soevereiniteit vertaalt de Online Trust Coalitie dit thema naar een praktisch handelingskader voor bestuurders, IT-verantwoordelijken, toezichthouders, serviceproviders en risk- en compliancefuncties. De OTC stelt dat digitale soevereiniteit niet draait om volledige autonomie of autarkie, maar om aantoonbare beheersing: inzicht in kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden, expliciete risicoafweging, uitvoerbare exit-mogelijkheden, onafhankelijke controle en heldere communicatie over restrisico’s en gemaakte keuzes. De OTC signaleert dat impliciet vertrouwen in digitale diensten onder druk staat. Geopolitieke spanningen, conflicterende rechtsstelsels, concentratie van leveranciersmacht en complexe beheerketens maken zichtbaar dat organisaties niet langer kunnen volstaan met contracten, certificaten of algemene toezeggingen. Wat haar aanpak bijzonder maakt, is hoe zij in een complexe publieke omgeving beweging creëert: door belangen zichtbaar te maken, partijen te verbinden en draagvlak te combineren met duidelijke keuzes. “Soms moet je als leider keuzes maken en stevig zijn: ik heb iedereen gehoord, maar we gaan toch die kant op.” Jolein Baidenmann is verandermanager en werkt met die insteek aan een overheid die openheid op een betekenisvolle manier probeert waar te maken. “Het is belangrijk dat een open overheid de samenleving in staat stelt om mee te denken, te controleren en gebruik te maken van de informatie die bij de overheid beschikbaar is.” Als manager Open Overheid en plaatsvervangend directeur Open Overheid bij het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) is Baidenmann bij uitstek de persoon om het concept ‘open overheid’ in praktijk te brengen. items.title: Call for Proposals: Artificial Intelligence in Collection Development and Acquisitions
items.raw_text: IFLA Acquisitions and Collection Development Section — Webinar, February 2027 The Acquisitions and Collection Development Section (ACD) of IFLA invites proposals for a webinar on the use of artificial intelligence in collection development and acquisitions, to be held in February 2027. AI tools are beginning to change how libraries build and manage their collections. Librarians are using them to analyze usage patterns, anticipate demand, and make the routine work of acquisitions and collection management faster and more responsive to what users need. This webinar is mostly about those opportunities. We also want to consider the risks, from selection bias to recommendations for outdated or nonexistent material to the environmental cost of large language models and open questions about author rights. We are sure that creative work is being done in this area and are looking forward to hearing from the librarians doing it. We are looking for case studies from libraries of different sizes, types, and regions. We are less interested in speculation about what AI might someday do than in accounts of what libraries are actually doing now: what has worked, what has not, and what others should know before trying something similar. Our focus is on AI as a tool for doing the work of collection development and acquisitions: informing selection and deselection, analyzing use, and improving acquisitions workflows. Introduction I often say that working in a university library in Nigeria isn’t for the faint-hearted, but leading one at a university of technology? That’s a calling all on its own. As the University Librarian at Ladoke Akintola University of Technology (LAUTECH), I operate in a space where passion, pressure, and purpose intersect. It’s a role that requires resilience, vision, and unwavering belief in the transformative power of information services, especially within an institution rooted in science and technology, situated in a region where infrastructure and funding can be unpredictable. items.title: Metropolitan Libraries Spotlight: How Nanhai Library Is Reconnecting Children with the Classics
items.raw_text: When a thousand-year-old novel has to compete with a 15-second video In Foshan, in the heart of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Nanhai Library serves a district of more than 3.7 million people, where local families, migrant workers, students, and seniors intertwine in a fast-moving, diverse community. It is also a community facing a very contemporary problem: as short-form video quietly absorbs every spare moment of screen time, deep reading is being pushed to the margins, even when the content at stake is centuries old. Rather than treat this as a lost cause, the library decided to meet children where their attention already lives. In April 2026, it launched Classics 101: Mental Models for Kids, a program built specifically for 10- to 12-year-olds — the exact age when children move from picture-to-text bridge books into more demanding reading. Making the classics legible again The challenge was concrete and specific. More than 60% of students in the first sessions admitted their biggest frustration was simple: they could not remember who everyone was or how all the characters connected. The semi-archaic language, sprawling character webs, and unhurried pacing of China’s Four Great Classical Novels were never designed to compete with instant gratification. This was not the first time that futures had been on the agenda at the KB. Already, a ‘Club Stof’ had brought together colleagues throughout the sector, keen to get to grips with ‘the uncomfortable uncertainty of the future’. items.title: Open science opens the process, not just the paper
items.raw_text: Beyond open access There is no doubt that open access has made major progress: about half of all papers are now published open access worldwide. However, making a paper readable is only the first step and “readable in the sense of open access doesn’t mean reliable or ready for replication,” remarked Prof. Robin Wilkening in the October 6th, 2026 webinar Beyond Open Access: Open Science Across the Entire Research Cycle , co-hosted by the Science and Technology Libraries Section and the Advisory Committee on Open Science and Scholarship . A scientific paper is only the tip of the iceberg. Beneath it are the research question, hypothesis, methods, protocols, instruments, data, code, and reviews that make the research possible. If these remain inaccessible, researchers are simply unable to replicate published findings. Wilkening, therefore, argues for open science across the entire research cycle, rather than focusing only on the final publication. Opening the research cycle Openness can begin with funding and continue through study design, data collection, analysis, publication, evaluation, and reuse. Researchers can pre-register their hypotheses and analysis plans, make instruments and tools open, deposit data and code in repositories, and use preprints to make findings available for discussion before the journal publication process is complete. items.title: Australian Public Libraries Statistical Report 2024–25
items.raw_text: Australians are using their public libraries in growing numbers, with visits, borrowing and participation in library programs continuing to rise despite increasing pressure on funding and staffing. The Australian Public Libraries Statistical Report 2024–25 , released by the Australian Library and Information Association (ALIA) and National and State Libraries Australasia (NSLA), provides a national snapshot of public library services and how Australians are using them. The figures tell a good news story, with Australian communities increasingly turning to their public libraries for collections, spaces, online services, programs and activities. Physical and online library visits increased by 8.5% in a single year, reaching a five-year high of more than 160 million visits. Public library collections were used almost 180 million times, while a record 434,000 library programs attracted more than 7.2 million attendees. Digital engagement also continues to grow, with digital collection use increasing by 80% over five years and Wi-Fi use almost doubling since 2021–22. Libraries are increasingly being used as places to meet, work and connect, with meeting-room use up 24% in the past year and 81% since 2021–22. Despite the steady increase in usage, public libraries are meeting this heightened demand within an increasingly constrained funding environment. items.raw_text: The troubling trend of book challenges and bans in libraries across the US continues. In 2025, 4,235 titles were banned or challenged at public, school, or university libraries, according to the American Library Association’s (ALA) State of America’s Libraries 2026 report. This figure was the second highest (following the record set in 2023) since ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom (OIF) began documenting censorship attempts in 1990. Behind each title is an author being professionally—and sometimes personally—targeted for the stories they have chosen to share. These works usually amplify marginalized voices such as abuse victims or those within the LGBTQ+ community. items.title: Refreshing for the Future
items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . items.title: Report: Minnesota Banned Book Bans, So Why Are Books Still Being Pulled From Shelves?
items.raw_text: From The Star Tribune: Two Minnesota schools have been among the national leaders in library book bans the past two years, despite a law here that first banned book bans in 2024. So, if it’s illegal, how did these books get pulled from shelves? The law lacks teeth, legal experts say, because it doesn’t lay out enforcement details or potential penalties. The law prohibits public libraries from banning books based on their messages and ideas. But it lacks enforcement, said Jane Kirtley, professor emerita of media ethics and law at the University of Minnesota. “The trouble with any kind of law dealing with restrictions on speech is that it’s not self-executing,” she said. It exists and people are supposed to follow it, but with no stated consequences or enforcement means, it can be violated without punishment, Kirtley said. [Clip] A growing number of states has enacted laws against book bans, said Sarah Lamdan, executive director of the American Library Association’s Office for Intellectual Freedom. Such laws protect readers’ rights and library workers, she said. About a dozen states have them, with several more considering their own ban ban. Some states have enforcement mechanisms or do things like limit funding when a law is broken, she said. And while some state laws may lack teeth, they still indicate that a state opposes book banning, said Lynn Oberlander, a partner with the law firm Ballard Spahr. items.title: OpenAlex Announces Launch of Trusted Journal Lists
items.raw_text: From an OpenAlex Post: Trust in science is under more pressure than it has been in a long time. Paper mills, hijacked journals, citation rings and a flood of machine-written manuscripts mean that “is this a real journal?” is now a question every reader, reviewer, funder and university has to ask. And the tools for answering it have not kept up. The traditional answer is a deny list. Something like the old Beall’s List : a roster of predatory journals, so you can filter them out of a search, an evaluation, a systematic review. We understand the appeal. Nobody wants to cite a paper mill by accident. But we’re not building a deny list, and we don’t think you want one either. Librarians have been making this case for a decade : deny lists are opaque , they go stale the moment they’re published, they’re a lawsuit magnet , and they land hardest on exactly the journals that can least absorb the hit… small, new, non-English, Global South. Beall’s List went dark in 2017 . The advice since then has been consistent: don’t filter out the bad, filter in the good. Use allow lists . [Clip] In the era of the legacy indexes, “approved” meant one thing: is it in the index? That made a kind of sense when a couple of companies ran the only lists. It makes less sense now, because different questions need different lists. We launched in September with twenty-two, and we keep adding more: there are 61 now . Google Scholar, library catalogues and generative AI are part of their everyday research routines. But what role do traditional subject-specific databases still play? And how well do students manage to find information, assess its quality and use it correctly in an academic context? These questions are at the heart of our new study (in German) „Zwischen Google Scholar und ChatGPT – Wie Wirtschaftsstudierende heute recherchieren“ (“Between Google Scholar and ChatGPT – How economics and business students conduct research today”). Between March and May 2026, we conducted an online survey of 908 economics and business students at German universities. Research habits are shifting The results show, first of all, that independent literature searching is routine for the vast majority of the surveyed students: 88.3 per cent have searched for literature or specialist information on their own, either frequently or occasionally. General search engines remain the most widely used tools, with 91.3 per cent of those with research experience using Google, Google Scholar or similar services sometimes or often. items.raw_text: Buffeted by Change, Researchers Seek Continuity and Investment: Results from the Ithaka S+R US Researcher Survey was written by: Chelsea McCracken Dylan Ruediger Ruby MacDougall From the Report’s Executive Summary: The research enterprise in the United States, established after the second world war, is experiencing massive disruption. US colleges and universities are grappling with federal and state disinvestment and intervention at a time when AI and other technologies are reshaping how research is conducted and its findings are communicated. As a result, researchers at US higher education institutions are operating in an unstable environment. Against this backdrop, the findings from our survey of 4,003 researchers, fielded in late 2025, demonstrate that they remain committed to carrying out essential work and that they are doing so in innovative ways—through collaboration, the creation of valuable educational experiences, and pushing knowledge towards the next frontier. While researchers don’t necessarily agree on how their sector should respond to the changing environment, our findings underscore the importance of stability, continuity, and sustained investment. Key Findings AI is producing deep divisions among researchers, but disclosure has emerged as a shared ethical baseline. items.title: New Data: PEN America Tracks Record School Book Bans (12,000) For a Single Year; Record Number of Unique Book Titles, at 7,000, Were Banned, as New State Laws, Artificial Intelligence, and Political Pressure Drives Censorship in Schools
items.raw_text: From PEN America: PEN America today reported nearly 12,000 book bans in public schools nationwide during the 2025-2026 school year—the largest number in a single year. New state censorship laws accounted for much of the increase, coupled with the use of artificial intelligence to remove books en masse including popular manga series and other graphic novels. In a report released to coincide with Banned Books Week, the latest accounting of book bans increased to 34,000 instances since PEN America began documenting the spreading book censorship crisis in schools in 2021. Texas recorded the largest number of book bans during the 2025-2026 school year (over 8,100), surpassing Florida (over 3,200), due to the impact of a censorial Texas law, SB13, which bans broad categories of books in schools. Florida had been No. 1 for three consecutive years. Most Banned Titles and Authors (PEN America 2026) The writers and free expression organization also reported a record number of unique titles banned in the last school year—more than 7,000—which impacted more than 4,000 authors, illustrators and translators, also a record number. In addition, researchers identified 114 school districts that had banned books over the year, the highest number ever for a single year according to PEN America ’s Index of School Book Bans. items.raw_text: Despite growing up in the bucolic New England town of Clossdale, Ash Hargreeves lives under a shadow of suspicion. When Ash was a baby, her mother died a fiery death soon after police discovered she was The Clossdale Killer, a serial killer whose victims were all popular high school girls. Years later, when five of Ash’s classmates disappear and townspeople discover dead bodies in the forest, all signs point to Ash as the most logical suspect. Over the course of one terrifying night, Ash teams up with her only two friends, Cassie and Jamie, to discover the real culprit, guided by their mantra WWJLCD (What Would Jamie Lee Curtis Do?). Laugh out loud funny with surprising twists, Beck Kubrick’s Dead Girls is a taut thriller that deftly upends the slasher genre. Critics have praised the graphic novel, with Kirkus Reviews hailing it as a “chilling slasher that effectively explores legacy, identity, confronting the past—and refusing to be defined by it.” We spoke to Kubrick about constructing the elaborate mysteries Dead Girls , playing with the framework of horror, and the “terrible feral” high schoolers at the heart of the story. items.title: E-Rate Under Threat: Take a Stand and Show Up for E-Rate
items.raw_text: After thirty years of keeping libraries online, the E-Rate program has seen its share of challenges. Just in the last two years, the program weathered the loss of support for hotspot lending and suffered through a Supreme Court Challenge . While the Supreme Court decision ultimately went in our favor, there is no time to sit back and relax for library advocates. In June, the Federal Communication’s Commission (FCC) launched a proceeding (officially, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking) that threatens to terminate this vital program. Now is the time to show up for E-Rate and tell the FCC what broadband access at your library means for your community. A Quick E-Rate Refresher One of four programs within the FCC’s Universal Service Fund, set up in the 1996 Telecommunications Act, the E-Rate program was established to ensure public libraries and K-12 schools have affordable access to advanced telecommunications (i.e., broadband and internet access). Today, E-Rate provides funding to almost three-quarters of public libraries to help offset monthly internet service costs and the costs for eligible technology necessary for making sure Wi-Fi is available throughout the building. How much are we talking about? Currently the program sends about $2.4 billion to public libraries and K-12 schools annually. items.title: Bringing Big Ideas Home: Reflections from PLA 2026 in Minneapolis
items.raw_text: The most valuable takeaway from my time at the Public Library Association Conference wasn’t just new ideas; it was a renewed sense of purpose. As the director of a small, rural library in Elba, Alabama, I was thrilled to receive a PLA scholarship to attend the conference in Minneapolis. PLA has supported our library in meaningful ways over the years, including a 2019 grant that funded a high school intern. That student is now about to graduate from college and, inspired by her experience at our library, is pursuing her MLS. Moments like that are a powerful reminder of the long-term impact of library work. Energy, Inspiration, and Hard Conversations I attended with a colleague from a neighboring library, and from the moment we walked into the Minneapolis Convention Center, the energy was contagious. We immediately felt welcomed, not just by the upbeat registration staff but by the shared sense of purpose among attendees. The opening session set the tone. Hearing from speakers, including Bryan Stevenson, was both inspiring and challenging. His remarks encouraged me to reflect more deeply on local history in my own community, including the possibility of researching and acknowledging difficult chapters like lynchings. I left with a desire to partner with our local historical preservation group to explore ways to honor and remember those stories. items.title: Building Acceptance and Community at PLA 2026
items.raw_text: My name is Lana Sweeting, and I was lucky enough to be selected for a 2026 PLA scholarship. I serve as an Adult Reference Librarian in Portland, Oregon, where much of my work focuses on serving the Black community through programming, collections, and outreach. While there were many sessions that were relevant and helpful to my everyday work, two in particular invigorated my work as a public librarian. First, I felt very drawn to the session “Every Story Matters, Every Body Belongs: Fat Inclusive Libraries.” The presenter, Amelia Mason, was absolutely wonderful and very knowledgeable on the subject. I was locked in from the very first slide, which simply said, “I Am Fat.” The honest and positive energy went up from there. Along with sharing quantitative data, Amelia discussed myths surrounding fatness, as well as history, race, fat acceptance and neutrality, and how these issues apply to library spaces and other spaces we regularly occupy. For example, Amelia noted that PLA shirts on the website only went up to size 3XL. After the session, I felt informed and inspired to take this information back to Multnomah County Library. The session included a resource booklist that inspired me to create a booklist and display for my own library and begin conversations around diversity audits of our catalog so we can make relevant materials more accessible. items.title: The Future Is Now: Black Men in Libraries
items.raw_text: I appreciated the chance to attend the PLA 2026 Conference. As an early-career librarian and MLIS student at the University of South Florida, I had no idea what to expect, but I am proud to report that I was not let down. I came to Minneapolis with a strong desire to learn more about public libraries, and I did just that. I learned more about how to strengthen library boards and foundations, how to protect queer and trans staff, and how to provide library services to those who are incarcerated. I am really happy with my experience. I attended various community-related sessions because it is so important to build relationships and have a sense of belonging, especially in today’s tumultuous political climate. This is also important in my Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) journey, where I promote positive connections, encourage librarians to embrace diversity, and build relationships with those around them. PLA was an amazing conference filled with experts who were welcoming and eager to answer questions from the audience. It was difficult to choose just one program to highlight because I genuinely enjoyed all the sessions. However, one stood out to me. My favorite was Black Men in Libraries: Our History, Our Heroes, and Our Horizon . items.title: ALA Launches Reporting Form for Incidents Against Immigrants in Libraries
items.raw_text: Acknowledgments: The author thanks Hayley Park of the University of Maryland for her contributions to language used in this article and Derek Wilmott of the University of Toledo for his assistance in developing the incident reporting form. Libraries across the country are navigating heightened immigration enforcement activity while trying to support community members and staff. Library leaders may face difficult decisions about how to respond to enforcement activity, address harassment, communicate with their communities, and protect patrons and employees, often with limited information about what other libraries are experiencing. Consider a public library responding to increased immigration enforcement activity in its community. Library leadership might consider issuing a public statement supporting immigrants but ultimately decide against it after consulting legal counsel, concerned that doing so could make the library a target. How can library leaders make decisions like this when much of the information available to them comes from anecdotal experiences or informal conversations with colleagues? Better data can help. The Services to Refugees, Immigrants, and Displaced Persons (SRIDP) Subcommittee is proud to announce the launch of the Incidents Against Immigrants in Libraries reporting form . items.title: Art for Everyone: How Public Libraries Expand Access
items.raw_text: Introducing children to viewing, creating, and enjoying art at a young age helps them appreciate it throughout their lives. Some children are exposed to various forms of art because it is part of their daily life or because they have easy access to museums and galleries in their community. But in many areas across the country, access to museums and art galleries can be cost prohibitive. That is where the public library comes in! While some museums, including the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., offer free admission, millions of people across the country do not have easy access to them. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. items.raw_text: Juno Dawson’s Survival Show begins with an irresistible premise: a reality TV show where contestants vie for one of five spots in a band, where each week the lowest-ranking contestant gets executed on live television. Dawson centers the book around Taryn Beck, a gutsy seventeen-year-old who’s survived a climate disaster and war and now lives in a refugee camp with her father and critically ill brother. When Taryn lands a chance to audition for Starmaker , the television show that has become a global phenomenon and launched past winners to superstardom, it seems like the best opportunity for her to provide her brother with desperately needed medical care. Yet when she begins rehearsing with her fellow contestants, Taryn must confront the challenge of collaborating and competing with contestants whose success could mean her death. Intrigue and romance quickly follow, and Dawson balances the gloom of her dystopian setting with a dark wit. Dawson previous books include This Book Is Gay and Clean, and critics have heaped similar praise on Survival Show . items.title: Autism Acceptance at All Ages
items.raw_text: Autism acceptance efforts have come a long way in recent years, and libraries are one of the key reasons why. As a librarian and the mother of two sons with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), I’ve witnessed this progress firsthand. In my capacity as the assistant director of the Beals Memorial Library (BML), I’ve seen how efforts to create more inclusive programs, services, and spaces can promote positive social change that dra-matically improves people’s quality of life, disabled or not. Through our “See Beyond the Spectrum” initiative, in recent years, BML has established new ASD-friendly programs, made our existing programs more accessible, updated our collections with texts by autistic writers, and established an autism caregiver support group. Our staff have gone through autism awareness training, and we’ve established partnerships with local organizations that serve autistic youth. Much of this workhas been supported by external grants, including generous funding from the ALA’s “Libraries Transforming Communities” initiative, which seeks to help libraries become more accessible to patrons with disabilities. Everything we’ve done has proved beneficial, both inside and outside of the library. Staff-patron interactions are more productive and less awkward. Families feel welcomed, and patrons with ASD feel comfortable being themselves when they visit. Community members are more knowledgeable about ASD and are actively talking about it. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Making the Invisible Visible: Advocacy at the Heart of Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Public libraries face no shortage of challenges today. Ongoing censorship efforts, increasing threats to staff safety, growing public distrust of institutions, and rapid technological change continue to reshape the work of libraries and the people who sustain them. In this environment, advocacy matters more than ever. That message came through clearly at the 2026 Public Library Association conference, where many sessions focused on helping librarians strengthen their advocacy skills. At the heart of every library are the workers who understand its value best and are often its strongest advocates. One session I attended, “Advocacy at the Core of ALA’s Next 150 Years,” featured Sam Helmick, Maria McCauley, Daniel Montgomery, and Lisa Varga. The panel offered practical strategies for advocacy, including using easy digital tools to contact legislators, participating in National Library Legislative Day, supporting legislation such as the Right to Read Act, and inviting elected officials into library spaces to see the work firsthand. Another standout session, “Advocacy Strategies for Getting Things Done,” featured Lisa Wells, Amanda Kordeliski, Tim Miller, Gail Oehler, and Kelly Sitzman from libraries across Oklahoma. Their discussion focused on the power of quiet advocacy. Quiet advocacy means building relationships with legislators before you urgently need their support. items.title: Creating Meaningful Connections Through Memory Cafés
items.raw_text: The 2026 Public Library Association conference featured many excellent sessions focused on programming and community engagement, but one that especially resonated with me was “Memory Cafés in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections,” presented by Christina M. Johnson, Allan M. Kleiman, and Susan H. McFadden. Before attending this session, I had heard of Memory Cafés but did not fully understand what they were, who they served, or how they could be integrated into library programming. By the end of the hour, I felt equipped with the knowledge and resources needed to successfully bring this type of program to my own library. The library where I work is within walking distance of two senior living apartment buildings, and our community of 16,000 is also home to several assisted living facilities. Older adults often make up the majority of attendees at our programs, so as the staff member responsible for adult programming, I attended PLA hoping to learn about meaningful services for this audience. The session began by defining the core audience for a Memory Café: people living with dementia, whether formally diagnosed or not, their caregivers, and volunteers interested in learning more. items.title: From Skeptic to Troublemaker: One Book Club Idea That Changed My Mind
items.raw_text: I’ll admit it: library book clubs make me instantly wary. People constantly ask libraries to offer them, only to never actually show up. And a book club for kids? Forget about it. They already have plenty of assigned reading at school. So when I attended Tanvi Rastogi’s session, “Speak Up: Using Middle Grade Books to Build Allyship Muscles,” I assumed it would be a low-stakes hour to slowly wake up and drink my coffee. Friends, I didn’t even need the coffee. I left energized. Rastogi’s book club model, Good Books Young Troublemakers (GBYT), is far more than a well-intentioned idea with a catchy title. It has its own website and 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status, a sign of just how thoroughly Rastogi developed this concept after first dreaming it up in the shower. She has created a turnkey model for anyone interested in starting a chapter. Each month features a thoughtfully selected recently published title, paired with a robust downloadable discussion guide. New chapter leaders can request a starter kit complete with stickers and bookmarks mailed directly to them. Best of all, it’s free, though donations are encouraged, and there’s a pretty fun sticker if you decide to support the work. So what is GBYT all about? items.title: Renewed and Reenergized: A Rural Librarian’s PLA 2026 Experience
items.raw_text: It was a true gift to attend the recent Public Library Association Conference in Minneapolis. It had been 12 years since I last attended PLA, and I had forgotten just how exciting and energizing it can be to gather with library workers from across the country. I am still reflecting on Dr. Benjamin’s perspective on AI, which she reframed, in part, as Ancestral Intelligence rather than Artificial Intelligence. The closing session with Lakota chef Sean Sherman felt especially meaningful as my library prepares to host the Americans traveling exhibit. The welcoming remarks from PLA President Brandy McNeil were timely and encouraging, and I was grateful to meet her and express my appreciation in person for the scholarship that made my attendance possible. items.title: Finding Connection and Community at PLA 2026
items.raw_text: Attending the PLA 2026 Conference in Minneapolis was an enriching experience in my professional development as a second-year MLIS student. I first learned about PLA while working as a Library Assistant and later as a Library Associate at my local public library system in Maryland. At the conference, I attended sessions on a range of topics, connected with library professionals, and shared time with fellow members of APALA. Having taken MLIS courses focused on children’s literature, multicultural resources, and the future of libraries, I was especially eager to learn more about early literacy services. In the session Intentional Early Literacy Outreach to Hispanohablantes , Andy and Carina from Arapahoe Libraries shared best practices and lessons from their efforts to connect with Spanish-speaking families. Although I am not a Spanish speaker, I appreciated the Spanish live captions throughout the presentation. One of the most valuable aspects of the session was the presenters’ candid discussion of what did not work. For example, they found that holding community meetings indoors at an apartment complex limited resident participation. Their experience highlighted the importance of time, persistence, and relationship-building with community management. items.title: “I Wanted To Write Something That Felt More Like A Hug” – DeAndra Davis On Her Enchanting Coming-Of-Age Novel
items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. items.title: Connections, Ideas, and a Little Hope: Reflections from PLA 2026
items.raw_text: I had the distinct honor of attending PLA 2026 in Minneapolis thanks to a PLA scholarship. As an eastern North Dakota native, Minneapolis is a familiar destination, but spending several days surrounded by thousands of energized library professionals made the city feel vibrant and new, despite the wind, cold, snow, and more wind. The connections, reunions, and conversations I experienced throughout the conference reminded me why gatherings like PLA matter. Alongside reconnecting with colleagues and making new professional connections, I left with fresh ideas, practical tools, and renewed optimism about the future of libraries. Several sessions stood out to me, both because of their content and because of the presenters who brought those ideas to life. One of the first sessions I attended was “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications,” presented by Mary Kapusta of Calgary Public Library. Kapusta was engaging, funny, honest, and refreshingly candid about both the successes and challenges of implementing a completely redesigned internal communications strategy across 23 library branches. What impressed me most was how scalable the ideas felt. Calgary Public Library serves nearly 1,000 employees, while my library employs roughly 30 staff members, yet many of the concepts felt immediately applicable. Instead, I left with a notebook full of starred ideas, half-written thoughts, and questions scribbled in the margins. Looking back, those messy notes reveal the sessions that stayed with me long after the conference ended. Conversations about internal communication, programming for older adults, and flexible, community-centered services challenged my assumptions and sparked new ideas for my own work. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content.
